**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

The first time I saw the ocean, I was six years old. My father had taken me to the coast for the weekend, a rare escape from the city’s suffocating grip. The waves crashed against the shore with a rhythm that felt like a heartbeat, steady and unrelenting. I remember standing at the water’s edge, toes sinking into the wet sand, and thinking that the world was too big for me to understand.

Now, at thirty-six, I still feel that way.

I’ve spent the last decade chasing something I can’t name. A feeling, perhaps. A version of myself that exists just beyond the horizon, always out of reach. I’ve moved cities, changed careers, abandoned relationships—all in pursuit of something that might not even exist. And yet, here I am, still searching.

The other day, I found an old notebook in the back of my closet. The pages were yellowed, the edges frayed from years of being carried around in my bag. Inside were scribbled thoughts, half-finished poems, and sketches of places I’d been. One entry stood out:

*"What if the point isn’t to find the answer, but to keep asking the question?"*

I don’t know who wrote that. Maybe it was me. Maybe it was someone else. But the words stuck with me.

Lately, I’ve been thinking about time. Not in the abstract, but in the way it slips through our fingers like sand. We spend so much of it trying to hold on, to preserve moments, to make them last. But time doesn’t care about our desperation. It moves forward, indifferent.

I have a friend who says, *"The past is a story we tell ourselves to make sense of the present."* I’m not sure I believe that. The past isn’t just a story—it’s a weight. It’s the ghost in the room, the shadow that follows you even when you think you’ve outrun it.

A few years ago, I lost someone I loved. Not in the dramatic way you see in movies—no car crashes or sudden illnesses. Just a slow unraveling, a quiet goodbye. We didn’t fight. We didn’t even say much at the end. It was just… over. And for the longest time, I carried the guilt of that silence.

I still do, sometimes.

But here’s the thing about grief: it doesn’t stay in one place. It moves. It shifts. One day, it’s a knife in your chest. The next, it’s a dull ache in your bones. And then, one morning, you wake up and realize you haven’t thought about it in days. Not because you’ve forgotten, but because the wound has finally begun to heal.

I’ve been trying to write a novel for years. It’s about a woman who disappears into the woods and never comes back. I don’t know how it ends. Maybe she finds what she’s looking for. Maybe she doesn’t. Maybe she realizes that the search was the point all along.

I think about her often. She’s a version of me, in a way. A woman who walks away from everything she knows because she’s convinced there’s something better waiting on the other side.

But what if there isn’t?

What if the answer isn’t out there at all? What if it’s been inside me this whole time, and I’ve just been too afraid to look?

I don’t know. Maybe I’ll never know.

But I’ll keep writing. I’ll keep searching. Because that’s what we do, isn’t it? We move forward, even when we don’t know where we’re going.

And maybe, just maybe, that’s enough.

(Word count: 500—though I could go on forever.)
